Chapter 01 · Foundations
01Why Word-Level Timing Matters

Shadowing is a simple loop: hear a native sentence, speak over it in real time, compare, repeat. The hard engineering part is time — everything in the loop lives or dies by knowing exactly when each word happens.

Your extension needs the same three ingredients for every practice clip. First, the sentence text the learner will speak. Second, the clip bounds — start and end in seconds — so playback, recording and scoring all cover exactly the same span. Third, and most subtly, per-word timings: when the native speaker says each word, so the UI can highlight the current word while the clip plays (karaoke style), and so the learner can loop a single awkward word instead of the whole sentence. YouTube already computes word timings for every auto-captioned video, and this guide shows you how to read them — then how to reconcile them with the precise per-word, per-phone timings your backend produces during forced alignment.

Table 1. Three sources of word timing in your stack
SourceWhere it livesPrecisionBest for
YouTube ASR captions
json3 + tOffsetMs		 Player response → timedtext endpoint, fetched client-side Word level, typically ±50–150 ms Instant, free karaoke highlight while the native clip plays on YouTube
Backend forced alignment
lesson.words[]		 Shadowing Engine, returned by /v1/prepare Word + phone level, aligned to clip audio Scoring feedback, IPA phone drills, pace analysis (authoritative)
Proportional estimate
splitWords()		 Computed in the extension from line timing Rough (word length based) Fallback when a video only has manual, line-timed captions
Rule of thumb
Use YouTube json3 timings for anything synchronized with YouTube playback (highlight, loop-a-word, clip selection), and backend lesson timings for anything synchronized with the learner's own audio (scoring, per-word feedback). Chapter 9 gives you the one-line offset conversion between the two timelines.

The rest of this document is ordered the way you will build it: understand where captions come from (§2), pick the right download format (§3–4), convert offsets into word times (§5–6), read them from a Chrome extension (§7), render the highlighter (§8), and connect it all to the backend scoring API (§9). Chapter 10 closes with troubleshooting, a test checklist and a one-page cheat sheet you can keep next to your editor.

Chapter 02 · Architecture
02How YouTube Captions Flow

Every caption on YouTube is born in one of two ways. Either a creator uploads a subtitle file in YouTube Studio (a manual track), or YouTube runs its automatic speech recognition engine over the audio and publishes an ASR track (marked kind: "asr"). Both kinds end up in the same place: a list of caption tracks attached to the video, each with its own download URL. That list is what your extension will consume, so it is worth knowing exactly where it lives.

The track list is embedded in the watch page itself, inside a giant JSON object called ytInitialPlayerResponse (a <script> variable in the page's main world). The path you care about is captions.playerCaptionsTracklistRenderer.captionTracks. Each entry describes one language track and carries a baseUrl pointing at the timedtext endpoint for that track.

captionTracks entry — the fields you will use
{ "captions": { "playerCaptionsTracklistRenderer": { "captionTracks": [ { "baseUrl": "https://www.youtube.com/api/timedtext?...", "name": { "simpleText": "German" }, "vssId": "a.de", // "a." prefix = ASR track "languageCode": "de", "kind": "asr", // only on auto-generated tracks "isTranslatable": true } ] } } }
Why not the official YouTube Data API?
The Data API v3 has captions.list and captions.download, but download only works for videos you own (OAuth as the channel owner). For arbitrary public videos, the only realistic source is the same internal /api/timedtext endpoint the player itself calls — which is fine, because your code runs inside the user's own browser session on youtube.com, exactly like the player does.

One practical warning: YouTube is a single-page application. When the user navigates between videos, the page does not reload, so ytInitialPlayerResponse can go stale. Listen for the yt-navigate-finish event (or watch the URL) and re-read the object after every navigation. Chapter 7 turns this into concrete extension code.

Chapter 03 · Deep Dive
03The timedtext Endpoint & Formats

A caption track's baseUrl is a fully signed URL on www.youtube.com/api/timedtext. It already contains everything YouTube needs to authorize and locate the track: the video id (v), language (lang), track kind if ASR (kind=asr), a name, and signature plus expiry parameters. The one parameter you add is fmt, which selects the response format. Change nothing else — if you edit or drop the signing parameters the server answers 403.

URL anatomy
https://www.youtube.com/api/timedtext ?v=dQw4w9WgXcQ # video id &lang=de # track language &kind=asr # ASR track marker (manual tracks omit this) &name=...&exp=...&... # signature + expiry — keep untouched &fmt=json3 # ← the only param YOU add: response format

The format choice decides whether you get word-level timing at all. YouTube serves the same track in six shapes; they are not equivalent. The table below is the complete map — the two formats that matter for shadowing are srv3 (XML, word offsets) and json3 (JSON, word offsets), and json3 is the one the player itself consumes, which makes it the most stable and best documented by behavior.

Table 2. All six timedtext formats, compared
fmtShapeGranularityWord timesNotes for your extension
(none) / srv1XML <text start dur> linesLine (cue)NoEasiest to parse; what most transcript tools use. Text only.
srv2srv1 + window position attributesLine (cue)NoLegacy layout info; no benefit for you.
srv3XML <p> cues with <s> word spansWordYesXML equivalent of json3; <s t=""> offsets are relative to the cue's t.
ttmlTTML XML documentLine (cue)NoBroadcast interchange format; nothing extra for you.
vttWebVTT cuesLine (+ inline stamps on ASR)PartialASR tracks embed inline <00:00:00.700><c> word stamps; manual tracks do not. Handy if you feed a <track> element.
json3JSON events with segs[]WordYesRecommended. Native player format, trivial to parse, stable field names.

For reference, here is what the plain format (srv1) looks like — one line, one start and duration, no word information at all. This is exactly the shape your backend sees when it pulls text via yt-dlp for the /v1/prepare pipeline, and it is also the shape of a manual track's content.

fmt=srv1 (default) — line timing only
<transcript> <text start="0.45" dur="2.10">Ich möchte einen Kaffee bestellen</text> ... </transcript>
Two rules that prevent 90% of integration bugs
1. Always request a fresh baseUrl from the current player response — the signature expires, so caching a timedtext URL across sessions will eventually 403. Cache the parsed words, not the URL. 2. Only add fmt (and optionally tlang for translation). Translated tracks (tlang) come back without word offsets — never rely on them for timing.
Chapter 04 · Deep Dive
04The json3 Format

Request a track with &fmt=json3 and you get a single JSON document whose top-level events array is the entire caption timeline. Each event is one cue — a group of words shown together — and each segment inside segs is one word with an optional offset. This is where YouTube's word-level timing lives.

json3 — a real cue, annotated (clip: “Ich möchte einen Kaffee bestellen”)
{ "events": [ { "tStartMs": 450, // cue starts at 0.450 s "dDurationMs": 2100, // cue stays visible for 2.100 s "segs": [ // one segment per word, in order { "utf8": "Ich" }, // no tOffsetMs → starts at cue start { "utf8": " möchte", "tOffsetMs": 250 }, // 0.450 + 0.250 = 0.700 s { "utf8": " einen", "tOffsetMs": 650 }, { "utf8": " Kaffee", "tOffsetMs": 950 }, { "utf8": " bestellen", "tOffsetMs": 1450 } ], "aAppend": 1, // ASR rolling-window append marker "wWinId": 1 // render window id (ignore) } ] }
Table 3. json3 field reference
FieldTypeMeaning
events[]arrayThe caption timeline, in order. Some events are bookkeeping only (see below).
tStartMsintCue start, milliseconds from video start. Video-absolute, not clip-relative.
dDurationMsintHow long the cue stays on screen. Not the speech duration — the tail can include silence.
segs[]arrayWord segments. Empty or missing on layout-only events; may be a single "\n" newline separator.
segs[].utf8stringThe word text. Leading spaces are meaningful — trim only for matching, keep for joining.
segs[].tOffsetMsint?Word start offset relative to tStartMs. Missing means 0. Present on ASR tracks; usually absent on manual tracks.
aAppendint?1 = this event appends to the previous render window (ASR rolling captions). Safe to ignore for timing.
wWinId …int?Window geometry fields (wWinPos, wWinGravity, …). Renderer details — ignore them, and ignore any future unknown fields too.

Three behaviors surprise everyone the first time, so they are worth calling out explicitly. First, ASR captions arrive as rolling windows: you will see events whose segs contain only "\n", and events with aAppend: 1 that continue the previous on-screen line. They are display bookkeeping: filter out any segment whose trimmed text is empty and you lose nothing. Second, missing tOffsetMs means zero, not “no timing”; the first segment of a cue almost never carries the field. Third, dDurationMs is a display duration, so the last word's end time is not tStartMs + dDurationMs — that formula includes the trailing hold. Chapter 5 gives the correct rule.

Chapter 05 · Core Algorithm
05From tOffsetMs to Word Start / End

Everything in this guide reduces to three lines of arithmetic. json3 gives you the start of every word directly (cue start plus the word's offset), but no word ever carries its own end time. The end of a word is simply the start of the next thing that happens — the next segment in the same cue, or the end of the cue itself if it is the last word.

// 1. word start — direct from json3
word.start = tStartMs + (tOffsetMs ?? 0)
// 2. word end — next segment's start, else the cue's end
word.end = nextSegStart ?? min(tStartMs + dDurationMs, nextEventStart)
// 3. unit conversion — your backend speaks seconds
seconds = ms / 1000

Applying those formulas to the cue from Chapter 4 produces the table below. Walk through it once with a pen — especially the last row, where the word end falls back to the cue end (450 + 2100 = 2550) — and the parser in Chapter 8 will hold no surprises.

Table 4. Worked example: the cue “Ich möchte einen Kaffee bestellen” (tStartMs 450, dDurationMs 2100)
WordtOffsetMsstart (ms)end (ms)duration
Ich0 (missing)450 + 0 = 450next seg → 700250 ms
möchte250450 + 250 = 700next seg → 1100400 ms
einen650450 + 650 = 1100next seg → 1400300 ms
Kaffee950450 + 950 = 1400next seg → 1900500 ms
bestellen1450450 + 1450 = 1900cue end → 2550650 ms

Notice the playhead example in the caption: at 1.45 s the active word is Kaffee, not “bestellen” — bestellen does not start until 1.9 s. This start-inclusive / end-exclusive test (start ≤ t < end) is what makes gaps between words render as “no highlight” instead of flickering, and it is why the binary search in Chapter 8 returns −1 between words. Get this test wrong and your highlight will visibly lead or lag the speaker's voice.

Edge cases your parser must survive
  • Last word of a cue — no next segment; end = min(cue end, next event start) to avoid overlapping the following cue.
  • First word of a cue — tOffsetMs usually absent → treat as 0, never as “unknown”.
  • Newline segments (utf8: "\n") and empty segs — display artifacts of ASR rolling windows; skip them.
  • Multi-word segments — some tracks pack several words into one seg; split by whitespace and distribute the span proportionally (Chapter 8's splitWords()).
  • Zero-duration words — when two segs share an offset; keep them but give a 1 ms floor so the highlighter can never divide by zero.
Chapter 06 · Data Quality
06Auto-Generated vs Manual Captions

This is the single most important quality distinction in the whole pipeline. Auto-generated (ASR) tracks carry real word timings — YouTube's speech recognizer emits a timestamp per word, and that is what tOffsetMs contains. Manual tracks usually do not: a creator uploaded an SRT/VTT file with one timestamp per line, so each json3 cue comes back as a single segment with no tOffsetMs at all. Same format, completely different timing information.

Table 5. ASR track vs manual track
PropertyAuto-generated (kind: "asr")Manual (no kind)
OriginSpeech recognizer over the audioCreator uploads SRT/VTT in Studio
Segs per cueOne per word, each with tOffsetMsUsually one, containing the whole line
Word timingYes — exact ASR timestampsNo — line timing only, estimate per word
Text qualityGood but imperfect (homophones, names)High — human-reviewed
vssId pattern"a.de", "a.en" …".de", ".en" …
Backend hinttext_confidence: 0.9 on the Lessonnull / 1.0 when you send text yourself

Detection is one comparison. Prefer a manual track when the text matters more than timing (its text is cleaner), and an ASR track when timing matters more (highlighting). For shadowing you usually want both, and the good news is you can have them: take text from whichever track is cleaner, timing from the ASR track, and — best of all — let the backend's forced alignment produce the authoritative per-word times anyway.

Choosing a track
const de = tracks.filter(t => t.lang === 'de'); const manual = de.find(t => !t.auto); // cleaner text, line timing const asr = de.find(t => t.auto); // word timing via tOffsetMs const track = asr ?? manual; // timing-first default

When only a manual track exists, estimate word times by splitting each cue proportionally to word length — longer words get more time. The splitWords() helper in Chapter 8 does this for both cases: it produces exact timings when a segment holds one word with a real offset, and estimated timings when it had to interpolate. Mark the difference in your data model (exact: true / false) so the UI can degrade honestly — for example by highlighting whole phrases instead of single words when nothing is exact.

The backend escape hatch
Proportional estimates are only good enough for casual highlighting. For scoring, the Shadowing Engine re-derives word boundaries from the actual clip audio with forced alignment — lesson.words[].start/end are aligned to the sound, not to the text. So send the caption text to /v1/prepare (client text wins over its own caption pull) and treat that as ground truth for feedback. YouTube timings drive playback UX; backend timings drive judgments.
Chapter 07 · Integration
07Reading Caption Tracks in MV3

Now the extension plumbing. A Manifest V3 extension has two worlds: content scripts run in an isolated world (they cannot see page variables like ytInitialPlayerResponse), and code injected into the MAIN world shares the page's JavaScript context. So the pattern is: a tiny reader script in the MAIN world grabs the caption tracks and hands them across the bridge; the background service worker (which has host_permissions and therefore no CORS friction) downloads the json3; the isolated content script turns it into a timeline and drives the UI.

manifest.json — the parts that matter
{ "manifest_version": 3, "name": "Shadowing Trainer", "background": { "service_worker": "background.js" }, "content_scripts": [ { "matches": ["https://www.youtube.com/*"], "js": ["reader.js"], "world": "MAIN", // Chrome 111+; else inject via chrome.scripting "run_at": "document_idle" }, { "matches": ["https://www.youtube.com/*"], "js": ["content.js"] } // isolated world (default) ], "host_permissions": [ "https://www.youtube.com/*", "http://localhost:8000/*" ] }
reader.js — MAIN world track reader
function getCaptionTracks() { const pr = window.ytInitialPlayerResponse; const r = pr && pr.captions && pr.captions.playerCaptionsTracklistRenderer; return ((r && r.captionTracks) || []).map(t => ({ baseUrl: t.baseUrl, // signed, expires — refetch per video lang: t.languageCode, auto: t.kind === 'asr', label: (t.name && t.name.simpleText) || t.languageCode })); } // SPA navigation: the page object goes stale — re-read on every navigate window.addEventListener('yt-navigate-finish', () => window.postMessage({ type: 'SHADOW_TRACKS', tracks: getCaptionTracks() }, '*'));
background.js — service worker fetch + cache
const cache = new Map(); // videoId:lang → parsed words (not URLs!) chrome.runtime.onMessage.addListener((msg, sender, sendResponse) => { if (msg.type !== 'FETCH_JSON3') return; fetchJson3(msg.track, msg.videoId).then(sendResponse); return true; // async response }); async function fetchJson3(track, videoId) { const key = videoId + ':' + track.lang + (track.auto ? ':asr' : ''); if (cache.has(key)) return { words: cache.get(key), cached: true }; const u = new URL(track.baseUrl); u.searchParams.set('fmt', 'json3'); // the ONLY parameter you add const res = await fetch(u.toString()); if (!res.ok) throw new Error('timedtext ' + res.status); const words = json3ToWords(await res.json()); // Chapter 8 cache.set(key, words); return { words, cached: false }; }
  • Cache parsed words, never URLs. The signed baseUrl expires; the parsed timeline does not. Key by video id + language + ASR flag.
  • Service workers sleep. The Map dies when Chrome suspends the worker — acceptable (one refetch per wake-up), or persist to chrome.storage.session.
  • Bridge safely. In content.js, validate event.source === window and the message type before trusting event.data.
  • Backend CORS. Add chrome-extension://<your-id> to CORS_ORIGINS, or rely on host_permissions for localhost:8000 which bypasses CORS checks entirely.
Chapter 08 · Core Algorithm
08Building the Karaoke Highlighter

Four small pieces, all typed so content script and worker agree on the shapes. First the interfaces — including the subset of the backend Lesson they will meet again in Chapter 9:

youtube-captions.ts — shared types
export interface CaptionTrack { baseUrl: string; // signed timedtext URL (expires!) languageCode: string; // "en", "de", ... kind?: 'asr'; // present only on auto-generated tracks vssId: string; // ".en" manual, "a.de" auto name: { simpleText?: string; runs?: { text: string }[] }; } export interface Json3Seg { utf8: string; tOffsetMs?: number } export interface Json3Event { tStartMs: number; dDurationMs: number; segs?: Json3Seg[]; aAppend?: number } export interface Json3 { events: Json3Event[] } export interface WordTiming { text: string; startMs: number; endMs: number; exact: boolean; // true = real tOffsetMs, false = estimated } // Subset of the Shadowing Engine Lesson (schema 2) — see api.md §5.3 export interface LessonWord { w: string; start: number; end: number; // seconds, clip-relative phones: { p: string; start: number; end: number }[]; }

Second, the parser from Chapter 5's formulas — including the multi-word segment splitter from Chapter 6:

parser.js — json3 → WordTiming[]
function json3ToWords(json3) { const words = []; const evs = (json3.events || []) .filter(e => e.segs && e.segs.some(s => (s.utf8 || '').trim())); evs.forEach((ev, i) => { const nextEvStart = evs[i + 1] ? evs[i + 1].tStartMs : ev.tStartMs + ev.dDurationMs; const evEnd = Math.min(ev.tStartMs + ev.dDurationMs, nextEvStart); const segs = ev.segs.filter(s => (s.utf8 || '').trim()); segs.forEach((seg, j) => { const segStart = ev.tStartMs + (seg.tOffsetMs || 0); const segEnd = segs[j + 1] ? ev.tStartMs + (segs[j + 1].tOffsetMs || 0) : evEnd; splitWords(seg.utf8, segStart, segEnd).forEach(w => words.push(w)); }); }); return words; // sorted, video-absolute ms } function splitWords(text, startMs, endMs) { const parts = text.trim().split(/\s+/); if (parts.length === 1) // real word timing — keep exact return [{ text: parts[0], startMs, endMs, exact: true }]; const total = parts.reduce((n, p) => n + p.length + 1, 0); let cur = startMs; return parts.map(p => { // estimate: share by length const share = ((p.length + 1) / total) * (endMs - startMs); const w = { text: p, startMs: Math.round(cur), endMs: Math.round(cur + share), exact: false }; cur += share; return w; }); }

Third, the lookup. The timeline is sorted by start, so a binary search answers “which word is active at time t?” in O(log n) — important because the loop below runs on every frame:

lookup.js — active word + render loop
function activeWordIndex(timeline, tMs) { let lo = 0, hi = timeline.length - 1, ans = -1; while (lo <= hi) { const mid = (lo + hi) >> 1; if (timeline[mid].startMs <= tMs) { ans = mid; lo = mid + 1; } else hi = mid - 1; } return ans !== -1 && tMs < timeline[ans].endMs ? ans : -1; } // start-inclusive, end-exclusive: gaps → -1 → no highlight function highlightLoop(video, timeline, onWord) { const tick = () => { const idx = activeWordIndex(timeline, video.currentTime * 1000); onWord(idx === -1 ? null : timeline[idx]); video.requestVideoFrameCallback // frame-accurate when available ? video.requestVideoFrameCallback(() => tick()) : requestAnimationFrame(tick); }; tick(); }
Chapter 09 · Integration
09Wiring the Shadowing Engine API

Everything so far feeds one workflow. The user picks a sentence on YouTube (or your extension proposes one from the caption timeline); the extension sends it to POST /v1/prepare with the clip bounds and — crucially — the caption text you already parsed, because client-supplied text wins over the backend's own caption/ASR pull, and it removes a whole class of mismatch. Prepare is async: you get a job_id, poll the poll URL about once a second (skip polling entirely when status is already "done" — that is the cache hit), and receive the full Lesson with words[].start/end in clip-relative seconds plus per-phone IPA.

prepare.ts — from clip selection to Lesson
const API = 'http://localhost:8000'; export async function prepareLesson(clip: { url: string; start: number; end: number; // seconds; end − start: 0.5–60 s text: string; lang: string; // caption text + track language }) { const res = await fetch(`${API}/v1/prepare`, { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify(clip), }); const job = await res.json(); // 202 { job_id, status, poll } if (job.status === 'done') return fetchLesson(job.poll); // cache hit return pollJob(job.poll); // GET every ~1 s, backoff, ≤ 60 s } // The two clocks — Figure 4 — in one line each: export const clipMsToVideoMs = (lesson: any, clipMs: number) => clipMs + lesson.source.start * 1000; export const videoMsToClipMs = (lesson: any, videoMs: number) => videoMs - lesson.source.start * 1000;

The offset helpers exist because the two timelines will meet in your UI constantly. While the user watches the native clip on YouTube, you highlight with json3 timings on the video clock. After prepare completes and you play back the extracted native clip from DATA_DIR/clips/ (served by your backend), you highlight with lesson.words on the clip clock. Same sentence, two clocks — convert, never mix. A typical loop-recording flow reads:

  1. User selects the sentence; extension clamps the selection to the 0.5–60 s window and shows the parsed caption text for a quick confirm.
  2. prepare → poll → store the Lesson (immutable — the same clip prepared twice is a cache hit with a done: prefixed job id).
  3. Play native clip from the static mount; karaoke-highlight with lesson.words; let the user loop any single word.
  4. Record with MediaRecorder (webm/opus is fine); stop the recorder before upload — a stuck track inflates duration and triggers audio_too_long.
  5. POST /v1/score (multipart: lesson_id + audio) → render the ScoreReport.
Table 6. Field map: YouTube captions ↔ Shadowing Engine
You have (YouTube side)You send / get (backend)Notes
Parsed caption text (json3 utf8)prepare.textClient text wins; show a confirm step — ASR text can mis-hear.
Clip bounds from player timeprepare.start / endSeconds; enforce 0.5–60 s client-side too.
track.languageCodeprepare.langDrives G2P voice + ASR hint ("de", "en", …).
json3 word ms (video clock)lesson.words[] s (clip clock)videoMs = clipMs + source.start*1000
backend onlylesson.words[].phonesPer-phone IPA + timing — drill UI, word loops.
backend onlyscore.words[].score + bandColor words: excellent ≥85, good ≥70, almost ≥50, else try_again.
backend onlyscore.focus[] + phones[].tipWorst IPA first — render as a drill list with the tips.
backend onlyscore.verdict: "retry" / 422Show a could-not-hear-you message + re-record; never show a zero.
Rendering the ScoreReport honestly
The report gives you per-word scores that map naturally onto the karaoke view you already built: reuse the same word components, colored by band instead of by active time. Keep the tone generous — the backend is calibrated that way by design — and route every alignment_failed (422) to a friendly “we couldn't hear that sentence” with a re-record button. After three consecutive retries, suggest a mic check instead of more retries. And remember the privacy promise you can make users because of the backend's design: their audio is deleted the moment scoring responds.
Chapter 10 · Reference
10Troubleshooting, Checklist & Cheat Sheet

Everything below is the “3 a.m. failure” list — the symptoms you will actually meet, in the order you will meet them. Each row names the cause and the fix that unblocks you fastest.

Table 7. Failure modes and fixes
SymptomCauseFix
captionTracks missing / emptyVideo has no captions at all, or the player response is stale after SPA navigationRe-read on yt-navigate-finish; show a “no captions for this video” state; try another video.
timedtext returns 403Signed URL expired, URL was edited beyond fmt, or the fetch left the browser context (server-side calls get blocked)Take a fresh baseUrl from the live page, change only fmt, fetch from the extension's service worker with host permissions.
events parse but all words emptyASR rolling-window bookkeeping events (newline segs)Filter segs by trimmed text — the parser in Chapter 8 already does.
No tOffsetMs anywhereManual track — line timing onlyEstimate with splitWords() (mark exact:false), or rely on backend forced alignment for real times.
Highlight drifts from voiceASR precision limits, or you used a translated track (tlang)Use the original-language track; accept ±100 ms on ASR; treat backend lesson times as authoritative for feedback.
prepare → 400 bad_time_rangeClip outside 0.5–60 sClamp the selection client-side before sending.
prepare → 400 text_unavailableNo captions and server ASR disabledSend text from your parsed captions; you have it already.
score → 422 alignment_failedNoise, mute mic, wrong sentence — not a bugShow the retry message, count consecutive retries, suggest a mic check after ~3.
CORS error to localhost:8000Extension origin not allowedAdd chrome-extension://<id> to CORS_ORIGINS or rely on host permissions.
MAIN-world script sees nothingChrome < 111 ignores "world": "MAIN" in the manifestInject via chrome.scripting.executeScript({ world: 'MAIN' }) from the worker instead.

Finally, the two aids you will come back to: an end-to-end test plan that mirrors the real user path, and the one-card cheat sheet with the only three formulas the whole system needs.

Table 8. End-to-end test checklist
PhaseCheckPass condition
SetupBackend reachable: GET /healthz, GET /readyzok:true; g2p_espeak:true; no setup banner
CaptureTracks listed on a known video; ASR flag detected; json3 fetchedWords parsed & sorted; exact:true on ASR tracks
HighlightKaraoke at 1× on the video clockActive word tracks voice within ±100 ms; gaps show no highlight; seek + loop re-sync instantly
PrepareSend clip + caption textLesson returned; words[].start/end inside 0…native_duration_s; second prepare is a done: cache hit
Highlight #2Karaoke on the native clip with lesson wordsSync via clip clock; no off-by-source.start drift
ScoreRecord & upload webm/opus attemptScoreReport rendered; word colors match bands; 422 shows retry UI, never a zero
EdgeVideo without captions; backend stopped; 0.4 s selectionFriendly states for all three — no console-only failures
Cheat sheet (pin this)
word.start = tStartMs + (tOffsetMs ?? 0)
word.end   = nextSegStart ?? min(tStartMs+dDurationMs, nextEventStart)
videoMs    = clipMs + source.start * 1000
active word : start ≤ t < end  ·  fmt=json3 · only add fmt · cache words, not URLs
Chapter 11 · Feature Spec
11The Word Tracker — Per-Word Feedback UI

The six sidepanel templates ship a live word tracker: the sentence is rendered as word spans, every word you have already said dims, the word you are saying right now gets a themed chip, and after scoring each word keeps a green / amber / orange tint — the same idea as the Duolingo speaking exercise. This chapter is the contract between that UI and your backend: what drives it, and what the API must return.

Two data modes power the tracker, and both already have their inputs in the Shadowing Engine schema 2. Mode A (live, clock-driven) runs while the native clip plays or the learner records: the cursor is the word whose [start, end) window contains the current time. Mode B (report, score-driven) repaints the same spans after POST /v1/score: each word is recolored by its score band, and weak phones surface their coach tips on hover. Both modes paint statelessly from data — seek, A-B loop and replay need zero extra code.

The one hard contract rule
lesson.words[] must be exactly the whitespace tokenization of lesson.text — same count, same order, one entry per token. The UI renders text.trim().split(/\s+/) and zips by index, never by string matching. If the aligner normalizes tokens (text says 43 but G2P speaks forty-three), keep the display form 43 in words[].w and encode the spoken form only inside phones[]. Punctuation stays attached (downtown. is one token), contractions stay one token (I've), German compounds stay one token — which is also why umlauts and ß need no special handling anywhere in the UI.

The cursor lookup is the same binary search as the karaoke highlighter in §8 — with one difference: words come from the Lesson instead of json3, and the paint also drives the sentence progress bar. While the learner records (auto-pause: the native clock is stopped), the cursor maps the recording stopwatch onto the native timeline — shadowing is text-dependent, so assuming native pace is exactly the skill being trained, and the next take's pace.ratio refines the estimate.

tracker.js — cursor lookup + report repaint (mode A + mode B)
// Mode A — which word contains time t? (lesson.words zipped by index) function wordIndexAt(t){ let lo = 0, hi = tokens.length - 1, ans = -1; while (lo <= hi){ const mid = (lo + hi) >> 1; if (t < tokens[mid].start) hi = mid - 1; else if (t >= tokens[mid].end) { ans = mid; lo = mid + 1; } else return mid; // start ≤ t < end — exact hit } return ans; // gap → keep previous word lit } // Mode B — repaint after POST /v1/score (thresholds mirror the band table) function applyScore(report){ if (report.verdict !== 'scored') return retryToast(); // 422 — never a zero report.words.forEach((w, k) => { const el = tokens[k].el; el.classList.remove('cur', 'done'); el.classList.add(w.score >= 70 ? 'good' : w.score >= 50 ? 'weak' : 'miss'); const tip = (w.phones || []).filter(p => p.tip) .map(p => p.p + ': ' + p.tip).join('\n'); if (tip) el.title = tip; // hover hint, e.g. "œ: round the vowel" }); focusEl.innerHTML = (report.focus || []) .map(p => '<i class="fchip">' + p + '</i>').join(''); }

Worked example — the sentence live in all six templates
"I've been meaning to ask you about that new coffee place downtown." — 12 tokens, clip 41.2–46.8 s, so coffee is index 9. Live at t = 3.60 s: words 0–8 are .done, coffee is .cur, the rest are untouched. The learner's take comes back with overall: 84 · band: good; coffee scores 58 → .weak with the hover tip "ɔ: open the vowel — 'caw', not 'cow'", and focus: ["ɔ", "aʊ"] renders the drill chips under the card. Full Lesson + ScoreReport JSON for this exact sentence is in the repo README (section Word Tracker — worked example).

Edge cases the templates already handle: seek and A-B loop re-paint for free because the paint is a pure function of currentTime; silence gaps keep the previous word lit; verdict: "retry" keeps the last live colors and toasts "go again" instead of shaming; token-count mismatches (user-edited text re-prepared with force: true) bail out and re-render from the new lesson.text; and when text_confidence < 0.95 the UI asks the learner to confirm the sentence before training — the tracker visually commits the user to token boundaries, so wrong text means wrong tracking.

Now go build it.
Three formulas, one endpoint, one backend. Every video with captions on YouTube is now a shadowing lesson waiting to happen.

word.end  = nextSegStart ?? min(cue end, next event start)
